path.title: Orchestration in production
path.summary: Schedules, sensors, idempotent loads, API ingestion, quality gates and alerting: what keeps a pipeline correct when it reruns, waits or fails. Airflow and pipeline behaviour is simulated by the labs; ingestion Python and SQL run for real.

lessons.title: Schedules, intervals and catchup
lessons.summary: Know which slice of data a run processes, and avoid an accidental backfill on deploy.

blocks.title: The mental model
blocks.body: Each DAG run has a logical date. With a data-interval timetable (Airflow 2 default for @daily) the run for 1 October covers 1 October 00:00 to 2 October 00:00 and starts once that interval is over. Airflow 3 schedules cron strings with CronTriggerTimetable by default: the run happens at the cron time and its logical date is that time, so a daily job that loads yesterday must compute yesterday from it.

blocks.title: Catchup
blocks.body: With catchup=True the scheduler creates one run per missed interval since start_date. Airflow 3 defaults catchup to False; in Airflow 2 it defaulted to True, which is how a new DAG with an old start_date launched months of runs at once.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.body: Filtering with the wall clock (datetime.now()) inside tasks. A retry or a backfill then loads the wrong day; use the run's data interval or logical date from the context.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: A @daily DAG with start_date 1 September and catchup=True is deployed on 1 October. How many runs are created?

visual.title: Schedules, intervals and catchup - visual walkthrough

steps.title: Declare the schedule
steps.body: schedule, start_date and catchup decide which runs exist.

steps.title: Read the interval
steps.body: The task receives the run's interval from the context instead of reading the clock.

steps.title: Deploy
steps.body: With catchup=False only the latest interval is scheduled; with True, one run per missed day.

steps.title: Rerun safely
steps.body: A retry or backfill of 3 September reloads exactly 3 September.

lessons.title: Sensors, pools and waiting well
lessons.summary: Wait for data without blocking workers, and cap concurrency on a shared resource.

blocks.title: The mental model
blocks.body: A sensor checks a condition (a file exists, a partition landed) until it is true or its timeout expires. In poke mode it holds a worker slot the whole time; in reschedule mode it frees the slot between checks; a deferrable sensor waits in the triggerer process. soft_fail=True turns a timeout into skipped instead of failed.

blocks.title: Sharing resources
blocks.body: A pool has a fixed number of slots; tasks assigned to it wait for a free slot, across all DAGs. Use one per rate-limited API or fragile database. When the trigger is data rather than time, schedule the consumer DAG on an asset (Dataset in Airflow 2) that the producer updates.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.body: Fifty poke-mode sensors waiting for files at night, each holding a worker slot, so the real work cannot start.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: The file never arrives. Should the run fail, or skip and let the next day try again? Which parameter decides?

code.source:
from airflow.providers.standard.sensors.filesystem import FileSensor

wait_for_file = FileSensor(
    task_id="wait_for_orders_file",
    filepath="/landing/orders/{{ ds }}.csv",
    mode="reschedule",
    poke_interval=300,
    timeout=6 * 60 * 60,
    soft_fail=True,
    pool="landing_fs",
)

visual.title: Sensors, pools and waiting well - visual walkthrough

steps.title: Check
steps.body: The sensor looks for the day's file.

steps.title: Release the slot
steps.body: In reschedule mode the task goes back to up_for_reschedule between checks.

steps.title: Give up gracefully
steps.body: After 6 hours the timeout ends the wait; soft_fail marks it skipped.

steps.title: Share the resource
steps.body: The pool caps how many such tasks touch the landing file system at once.

lessons.title: Idempotent loads and backfills
lessons.summary: A load you can rerun for the same day without duplicating or losing rows.

blocks.title: The mental model
blocks.body: Every production task will run twice one day: a retry after a timeout, a manual rerun, a backfill. An idempotent load leaves the same table whatever the number of runs. Two patterns: replace the slice the run owns (delete then insert the day, or overwrite that partition, in one transaction), or MERGE on the business key so repeated rows update instead of inserting.

blocks.title: Watermarks
blocks.body: Incremental loads remember the highest updated_at they have committed. Read the watermark, load rows above it, write them idempotently, and only then store the new watermark.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.body: INSERT INTO ... SELECT for the day without removing the previous attempt first: every retry adds the day again.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: The example removes the day and inserts it again. What happens if the run fails between the two statements, and how does a transaction help?

visual.title: Idempotent loads and backfills - visual walkthrough

steps.title: Own a slice
steps.body: The run owns exactly one day of the target.

steps.title: Replace it
steps.body: Delete and insert inside one transaction: a failure leaves the previous state.

steps.title: Or merge
steps.body: MERGE on customer_id updates existing rows and inserts new ones.

steps.title: Rerun
steps.body: A second run produces the same table: no duplicates, nothing lost.

lessons.title: Ingesting from an API in production
lessons.summary: Pagination, rate limits, retries and a watermark committed after the write.

blocks.title: The mental model
blocks.body: A production ingestion follows every page (cursor first, offset only when the data cannot move), retries only transient answers (429, 502, 503, 504, timeouts) with exponential backoff and jitter and honours Retry-After, fails fast on 400, 401, 403 and 404, writes each batch idempotently, then advances the watermark. New fields in the payload are schema drift: decide explicitly whether to evolve the table.

blocks.title: What this lab shows
blocks.body: The API Lab serves a simulated API on 127.0.0.1 with seeded pages and faults; your ingest.py runs for real as trusted local Python and writes real DuckDB tables in bronze. Missions api-rate-limited-events and api-incremental-orders check the request log and the rows.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.body: Saving the watermark from the API response before the write commits. If the write fails, the next run starts after rows that were never stored.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: Which statuses does your client retry, how long does it wait at most, and what does it do after the last attempt?

visual.title: Ingesting from an API in production - visual walkthrough

steps.title: Classify the answer
steps.body: Only transient statuses are retried.

steps.title: Honour the server
steps.body: Retry-After, when present, is the delay to use.

steps.title: Back off
steps.body: Otherwise the delay doubles per attempt, capped, with jitter so clients do not retry in step.

steps.title: Commit then advance
steps.body: Write the batch, then store the new watermark.

lessons.title: Data quality gates
lessons.summary: Validate before publishing: quarantine bad rows and stop the run when the batch is not trustworthy.

blocks.title: The mental model
blocks.body: Quality checks work at two levels. Row rules (a non-null key, a positive amount, a known status) route failing rows to a quarantine table with the reason. Batch rules (row count within the usual range, no duplicate keys, the share of quarantined rows under a threshold) decide whether the batch is published at all. Publish gold only after the gate passes, so consumers never see a half-checked day.

blocks.title: On the platforms
blocks.body: dbt tests, Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines expectations (warn, DROP ROW, FAIL UPDATE) and Great Expectations-style suites are the same idea. The Pipeline Lab compiles the lesson's pipeline source with a bounded AST compiler, never eval or exec.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.body: Dropping invalid rows silently. The run is green, the totals are wrong, and nobody can find out which rows went missing.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: Two percent of today's rows fail the amount rule; usually it is 0.1 percent. Publish or stop?

code.source:
WITH checked AS (
    SELECT *,
           CASE WHEN customer_id IS NULL THEN 'missing customer'
                WHEN net_amount <= 0 THEN 'non-positive amount' END AS reason
    FROM source.orders
)
SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE reason IS NULL) AS valid_rows,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE reason IS NOT NULL) AS quarantined_rows,
       round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE reason IS NOT NULL) / count(*), 1) AS quarantined_pct
FROM checked;

steps.title: Row rules
steps.body: Each row gets a reason when it breaks a rule.

steps.title: Split
steps.body: Valid rows go on; the others go to quarantine with their reason.

steps.title: Batch rule
steps.body: The quarantined share is compared with a threshold.

steps.title: Publish or stop
steps.body: Gold is refreshed only when the gate passes.

lessons.title: Timeouts, retries and alerting
lessons.summary: Retry what is transient, time out what hangs, and alert a human only when action is needed.

blocks.title: The mental model
blocks.body: Retries handle transient failures; they need an attempt to end, so every task also needs a timeout shorter than its slot in the schedule. After the last retry the failure must stay visible: the run fails and an alert reaches the owner with the task, the run and a link to the logs. A watcher or failure-only task can send the alert, but it must not turn the run green.

blocks.title: Good alerts
blocks.body: Alert on symptoms someone must act on (a failed run, a late table, a quality gate stop), with a runbook line saying what to check first. Too many alerts teach people to ignore them.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.body: Retrying a slow task: retries restart the same slow work. Fix the slowness or raise the timeout; retry only transient errors.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: A task has retries=3, retry delay 5 minutes and no timeout; it hangs. When does anybody find out?

visual.title: Timeouts, retries and alerting - visual walkthrough

steps.title: Bound each attempt
steps.body: A 30-minute timeout ends a hung attempt.

steps.title: Retry transient errors
steps.body: Two retries, five minutes apart.

steps.title: Do not retry slowness
steps.body: A timed-out attempt is not retried here: the same work would hang again.

steps.title: Tell a human
steps.body: After the last attempt the run fails and the on-call address is notified.
